name: test
one_line: check file types and compare values (also written as [ ... ])
plain: `test` answers yes/no questions: does this file exist, is this string empty, is 5 bigger than 3? It prints nothing; it sets its exit status to 0 for true and 1 for false. Shell scripts use it inside if and while.
The square-bracket form `[ ... ]` is the same command with a closing ] required. In bash, `[[ ... ]]` is a related built-in with extra features (pattern matching and no word-splitting surprises).
when: Check whether a file or directory exists before using it.
Compare numbers or strings in a script.
Decide in a script whether you are root.

examples.title: Does the file exist?
examples.explain: -f is true for a regular file. && runs echo only when the test is true.

examples.title: Bracket form in an if
examples.explain: Spaces inside the brackets are required.

examples.title: Is the string empty?
examples.explain: -z true if length zero; -n true if not zero.

examples.title: Compare strings
examples.explain: Use = for strings (with spaces around it) and always quote variables.

examples.title: Compare numbers
examples.explain: -eq -ne -lt -le -gt -ge are for numbers. Using > or < compares nothing useful in [ ].

examples.title: Combine tests
examples.explain: Chain with && or use -a / -o inside (older style).

examples.title: Am I root?
examples.explain: id -u prints your numeric user id; root is 0.

examples.title: Newer than?
examples.explain: -nt is newer than, -ot older than, -ef the same file.

mistakes: Missing spaces: [ -f file] or [-f file] fail.
Not quoting variables: an empty variable removes the argument and breaks the test.
Using = for numbers or -eq for strings.
Using > inside [ ] and creating a file named after the number.
Forgetting that [[ ]] is bash only: scripts for sh must use [ ].
